subject: Architecture
title: The Flatiron: New York's Oddest Tower
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Flatiron: New York's Oddest Tower.

hook.text: In 1902, a 22-story triangle appeared at the intersection of Broadway and Fifth Avenue.

buildup.text: The Flatiron Building was only six feet wide at its narrow end — critics said wind would topple it.

discovery.text: Its steel frame made the narrow shape possible. Stone walls that thin would have crumbled instantly.

twist.text: Wind swirling around the building lifted women's skirts. Police had to patrol the intersection.

climax.text: Photographers loved its dramatic shape. It became the most photographed building in early New York.

punchline.text: Too thin to stand? It's been standing for over 120 years.

quiz.question: Why did critics doubt the Flatiron Building would survive?
options: Its foundation sat on unstable marshland
They believed wind would topple such a narrow structure

details.summary: The Flatiron Building, completed in 1902, fills a triangular plot at Broadway and Fifth Avenue with a dramatically narrow wedge shape. At 22 stories, it was one of New York's tallest buildings and became an icon for its unusual form and wind-tunnel effect on pedestrians below.
details.whyItMatters: The Flatiron proved that skyscrapers could be sculptural landmarks, not just tall boxes. Its distinctive silhouette became one of New York's most photographed buildings and showed that site constraints could inspire iconic design.
takeaways: Completed in 1902 on a triangular lot in Manhattan
Its wedge shape created a distinctive sculptural silhouette
Wind effects around the building became legendary

faq.question: Why is the Flatiron Building shaped like a triangle?
faq.answer: The lot where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue at 23rd Street creates a narrow triangular plot. Architect Daniel Burnham designed the building to fill the entire site, resulting in the distinctive wedge that narrows to just two meters at its sharp end.

faq.question: What is the Flatiron's wind effect?
faq.answer: The wedge shape splits and accelerates wind around the building, creating strong gusts at street level. In the early 1900s, police reportedly had to disperse men who gathered to watch wind lift women's skirts — giving rise to the phrase 'twenty-three skidoo.'
